title.text: GDL and the early bird road

why_how.text: The GDL Program phases in privileges and extends practice so new drivers build skill before full freedom at eighteen.
Option A ties the youngest drivers to an instructor, a course and a validation step before any practice.

scenario.text: Maya turns sixteen and wants to start on the early bird road.

reasoning.text: She needs consent and course enrollment; her instructor buys the special learner permit after she supplies her documents, and she passes the knowledge and vision tests.

result.text: After six full hours in a dual-control car, she gets the permit validated at a Driver Testing Center before practicing.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the special learner permit can be used for practice as soon as the instructor buys it.

correction.text: A permit cannot be used for practice until an MVC Driver Testing Center validates it, which on Option A happens only after the course.

prompt.text: Maya finished her six-hour course on Friday. May she practice on Saturday before returning to the MVC?

answer.text: No. She must first get the permit validated at a Licensing Center with a Driver Testing Center.

rationale.text: A permit may not be used for practice until an MVC Driver Testing Center has validated it.

lines.text: New drivers earn privileges in steps.

narration.text: This lesson opens the part of the New Jersey manual that shapes every new driver's first years on the road. New Jersey began its Graduated Driver License Program, usually called GDL, in two thousand one. The idea is simple: instead of handing first-time drivers every privilege at once, the program phases those privileges in and stretches out the practice time. It also sets eighteen as the minimum age for an unrestricted basic license. There are three roads through the program. We start with Option A, the early bird road, which is the youngest starting point and the only one built around a driving school instructor.

lines.text: Phases in privileges for first-time drivers.

narration.text: Let us look at the program's purpose more closely, because it explains every rule that follows. The Graduated Driver License Program does three things at once. It phases in privileges, so a new driver earns freedom step by step instead of all at the start. It extends practice time, so skills are built under supervision before anyone drives alone. And it sets a floor of eighteen for the unrestricted basic license, no matter how early someone begins. When a question asks about the youngest age for a full, unrestricted license in New Jersey, the answer comes from this rule. Starting younger changes the road you take, not that final age of eighteen.

lines.text: Special learner permit at sixteen or older.
Enrolled in an approved behind-the-wheel course.

narration.text: Option A is called the early bird road because it is where the youngest drivers begin. It starts with a special learner permit, available at age sixteen or older. Three things come together at the start: the permit itself, signed consent from a parent or guardian, and enrollment in an approved behind-the-wheel training course. Before the permit can be bought, the applicant fills out the form and supplies six points of ID, proof of home address and proof of Social Security number. Keep the order in mind. The paperwork and the course enrollment come first, and the permit follows from them.

lines.text: An approved instructor buys the permit.
Applicant passes knowledge and vision tests.

narration.text: Here is a detail that makes Option A unusual. The applicant does not walk in and buy the special learner permit alone. An approved driving instructor buys it. The applicant still has to pass the knowledge and vision tests, just like anyone else seeking a permit. Once the instructor buys the special learner permit, it stays valid for two years. That two-year window gives a young driver time to finish the course and start practicing without rushing. If a question asks who purchases the special learner permit, think instructor, and if it asks how long the permit lasts, think two years.

lines.text: Six full hours behind the wheel.
Time at the MVC does not count.

narration.text: The approved course behind the special learner permit has a precise shape. It is six full hours of behind-the-wheel teaching, given in a car with dual controls, so the instructor has a second set of controls beside the student. Notice the word full. Time spent at the MVC buying the permit does not count toward those six hours, and neither does time spent testing there. Only teaching behind the wheel counts. This matters because people sometimes assume a morning at the motor vehicle office chips away at the course. It does not. The six hours are pure instruction in the dual-control car.

lines.text: Then validation at a Driver Testing Center.

narration.text: This is the step learners most often skip in their heads. Finishing the six-hour course does not, by itself, let the new driver start practicing. After the course and before any practice, the special learner permit holder must get the permit validated at a Licensing Center that has a Driver Testing Center. The broader rule is the same for every permit: it may not be used for practice driving until an MVC Driver Testing Center has validated it. On Option A, the early bird road, an approved instructor must purchase the Special Learner Permit and the MVC validates it only after behind-the-wheel training completion. Buy, train, validate, then practice.

Here is a quick check: Maya is sixteen, her instructor bought her special learner permit, and she finished her six full hours of behind-the-wheel teaching on Friday. Her aunt offers to take her out for practice on Saturday morning, before Maya has been back to the MVC. Is that allowed? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. After the course and before practicing, Maya must get her permit validated at a Licensing Center that has a Driver Testing Center. A permit cannot be used for practice driving until it has been validated, so Saturday's drive has to wait for that visit.

title.text: The early bird road so far

lines.text: GDL began in two thousand one.

narration.text: Let us pull this lesson together. New Jersey's Graduated Driver License Program began in two thousand one to phase in privileges, extend practice and hold the unrestricted basic license until eighteen. Option A, the early bird road, starts at sixteen with a special learner permit, a parent or guardian's signed consent, and enrollment in an approved course. The instructor buys the permit, which stays valid for two years, after the applicant supplies the form, six points of ID, proof of address and proof of Social Security number. Six full hours of dual-control teaching come next, then validation, and only then practice. Next, we follow the practice itself.

why_how.text: Time and hours are separate minimums, so practice must satisfy both before the road test.
Each stage has its own age, so being ready early does not skip a step.

scenario.text: Sam starts Option A at sixteen and logs fifty supervised hours, ten at night, over six months.

reasoning.text: With no suspensions, his supervisor's certification and a passed road test, he still needs to be seventeen for the probationary license.

result.text: After a year of probationary driving he is eighteen and visits a Licensing Center to upgrade.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing probationary restrictions end automatically after the twelve-month period.

correction.text: The driver must visit a Licensing Center to upgrade; otherwise the restrictions keep applying and police can enforce them.

memory_support.text: Six months, fifty hours, then upgrade.

prompt.text: Aisha finished probation long ago but never visited the MVC. Do her restrictions still apply?

answer.text: Yes, until she visits a Licensing Center to upgrade.

rationale.text: Without the upgrade visit after the probationary period, restrictions keep applying and police can enforce them.

narration.text: Once a special learner permit is validated, the main work of Option A begins: supervised practice. This lesson follows a young driver from that first practice drive all the way to the basic license. Along the way there are minimum lengths of time, a minimum number of hours, a form that proves the practice happened, a road test, a probationary stage and, at the very end, one more visit to the MVC that many drivers forget. Each step has its own age or time rule, and questions love to swap them. We will line them up in order so each one stays attached to the right stage.

lines.text: At least six months of practice.
At least fifty hours in total.
Ten of those hours in darkness.
Red GDL decals on the vehicle.

narration.text: Option A supervised practice has two separate minimums, and both must be met. First, it lasts at least six months. Second, it must total at least fifty driving hours. Of those fifty hours, ten must be driven in darkness, so the night hours sit inside the fifty rather than on top of them. During this whole period, the vehicle displays the red GDL decals. A driver who piles up fifty hours in a short burst has not finished, because the six-month clock still runs. A driver who waits six months but logs far fewer hours has not finished either. Time and hours both count.

lines.text: Applicant hands it in at licensing.

narration.text: Practice has to be documented, and New Jersey uses a single form for it: the Certification of Supervised Driving. The person who fills it out is a parent, guardian or supervising driver who rode along during practice, not the new driver and not the instructor. The new driver, the applicant, is the one who hands it in, and that happens at the time of licensing. So two different people touch the form. The adult completes it, and the young driver delivers it when it is time to be licensed. If a question asks who fills out the record of supervised practice, look for the parent, guardian or supervising driver.

lines.text: Six clean months of supervised driving.

narration.text: The next milestone on Option A is the probationary license. Three conditions must all be true. The driver needs six months of supervised driving without any suspensions or postponements, so the clock has to run cleanly. The driver must pass the MVC road test. And the driver must be at least seventeen years old. Notice how this connects to the start of the road: a driver who begins at sixteen and practices cleanly for six months can reach the road test, but the probationary license still waits until seventeen. Being ready early does not move the age rule, so plan the timeline around both conditions.

lines.text: At least one year of probation.
Basic license at eighteen or older.

narration.text: Here is the trap at the end of the road. After the probationary license, Option A requires at least one year of unsupervised driving under probationary restrictions, and the basic license comes at age eighteen or older. Many people assume that once the standard twelve-month probationary period is over, the restrictions simply fall away. They do not. The driver must visit a Licensing Center to upgrade to a basic license. Until that visit happens, the probationary restrictions keep applying, and police can enforce them. Finishing the year is necessary, but the upgrade visit is what changes the license.

Here is a quick check: Aisha got her Option A probationary license, drove unsupervised under the restrictions for well over a year, and is now past eighteen. She never went back to the MVC, because she assumed her license upgraded on its own. Are her probationary restrictions still in force? Work it out before reading on. Yes, they are. After the standard twelve-month probationary period, the driver must visit a Licensing Center to upgrade to a basic license. Without that visit, the probationary restrictions keep applying, and police can enforce them. Aisha needs to make the upgrade visit.

lines.text: Six months, fifty hours, ten at night.
Road test and seventeen for probation.

narration.text: Let us pull this lesson together. On Option A, supervised practice lasts at least six months and at least fifty hours, with ten of those hours in darkness and the red decals on the vehicle. A parent, guardian or supervising driver fills out the Certification of Supervised Driving, and the applicant hands it in at licensing. The probationary license needs six clean months, a passed road test and an age of at least seventeen. Then comes at least a year of unsupervised driving under restrictions, the basic license at eighteen or older, and the upgrade visit that ends the restrictions. Next, we compare the two other roads.

why_how.text: Older starters skip the instructor and course, so the examination permit begins after the tests alone.
The adult road shortens supervised practice to three months, which is the key contrast with the younger roads.

scenario.text: Carlos, older than twenty-one, passes the knowledge and vision tests and gets an examination permit.

reasoning.text: He is on Option C, which lists three months of supervised practice and no practice-hour minimum.

result.text: After three clean months and a road test, he drives unsupervised for a year before the basic license.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking every road requires fifty supervised hours.

correction.text: Options A and B require fifty hours, but the Option C chart lists only three months with no hour minimum.

memory_support.text: Seventeen for B, twenty-one for C.

prompt.text: Carlos, past twenty-one, got an examination permit. Does he need fifty logged hours before his road test?

answer.text: No. Option C lists three months of supervised practice with no hour minimum.

rationale.text: The fifty-hour minimum belongs to Options A and B; the adult road chart lists only three months.

title.text: Two more roads to a license

narration.text: This lesson covers the other two roads through New Jersey's Graduated Driver License Program. Option B is the young adult road, and Option C is the adult road. Both begin differently from the early bird road you just learned. There is no special learner permit, no instructor buying it and no required six-hour course. Instead, each road starts with an examination permit after the applicant passes the knowledge and vision tests. What changes between the roads is the starting age and how much supervised practice comes before the road test. Keep comparing each rule back to Option A, because that comparison is where most questions live.

lines.text: Examination permit at seventeen or older.
Pass knowledge and vision tests first.

narration.text: Option B begins with an examination permit at age seventeen or older. To get it, the applicant passes the knowledge and vision tests. If the applicant is still under eighteen, a parent or guardian must consent. Any New Jersey resident aged seventeen or older who is not suspended can get an examination permit. Those knowledge test and vision screening results are good for two years, the same length of time a special learner permit stays valid once an instructor buys it. So the two-year figure belongs to both the special learner permit and the test results, and questions sometimes ask about one using the other.

lines.text: Examination: no student status, no instructor.

narration.text: Two permits sound alike, and the difference between them is a favorite on practice questions. A special learner permit is tied to a student in a training course with an instructor. That is why Option A requires enrollment in an approved behind-the-wheel course. An examination permit needs neither student status nor an instructor. A New Jersey resident who is seventeen or older and not suspended can simply pass the tests and get one. So if a question describes someone with no driving school at all, the permit in play is the examination permit. If it describes a student and an instructor, it is the special learner permit.

lines.text: Ten of those hours after dark.
Road test, a year, then basic.

narration.text: Once the examination permit is in hand on Option B, practice looks very much like Option A. Option B also requires at least six months of supervised practice, with at least fifty hours in total, and ten of those hours after dark. After that, the driver passes a road test. The road then ends with the basic license at age eighteen or older, after one year of unsupervised driving under probationary restrictions. So the young adult road differs from the early bird road at the start, with no instructor and no course, but it shares the same six months, the same fifty hours and a year of probation.

lines.text: Examination permit at twenty-one or older.
One year before the basic license.

narration.text: Option C is the adult road, for people who start at twenty-one or older. It begins the same way as Option B, with an examination permit after passing the knowledge and vision tests. The big change is practice time. Option C requires at least three months of supervised practice, with no suspensions or postponements, before the road test. After the road test comes one year of unsupervised driving before the basic license. So adults get a shorter supervised stretch, but they still serve the year of unsupervised driving before the basic license is issued, just like drivers on the younger roads.

lines.text: Option C: three months, no hour minimum.
Options A and B: six months, fifty hours.

narration.text: Here is where the adult road trips people up. The Option C chart lists only three months of supervised practice, and it lists no practice-hour minimum at all. Options A and B both demand at least six months and at least fifty hours, with ten of them after dark. It is tempting to carry that fifty-hour figure over to adults, but the Option C chart does not include it. When a question pairs three months with fifty hours, or six months with Option C, treat it as a swap. Three months and no hour minimum belongs to the adult road; six months and fifty hours belong to the younger roads.

lines.text: Fifty hours before the road test?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Carlos is older than twenty-one and has never held a license. He passes the knowledge and vision tests and gets an examination permit. His friend tells him he now needs six months and fifty logged hours before the road test. Is his friend right? Work it out before reading on. No. Carlos is on Option C, the adult road. Its chart lists only three months of supervised practice, with no suspensions or postponements, and no practice-hour minimum. After the road test, he still has one year of unsupervised driving before the basic license.

lines.text: Option B: seventeen, six months, fifty hours.

narration.text: Let us pull this lesson together. Option B, the young adult road, starts with an examination permit at seventeen or older after the knowledge and vision tests, with consent if under eighteen. It asks for at least six months and fifty supervised hours, ten after dark, then a road test and a year of probation before the basic license at eighteen. Option C, the adult road, starts at twenty-one, lists three months of practice with no hour minimum, then a road test and a year of unsupervised driving. Neither road uses an instructor, and test results last two years. Next come the restrictions that apply while driving.

why_how.text: The late-night ban covers every GDL stage, so probationary drivers stay off the road too.
The phone ban is total because it covers hand-held, hands-free and every other device.

scenario.text: Eli, under twenty-one with a probationary license, finishes work at midnight.

reasoning.text: The prohibited hours apply to him, but the work exemption allows driving if he carries the signed letterhead certification.

result.text: He keeps the certification in the car and drives home legally during those hours.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking hands-free phones are allowed for GDL drivers.

correction.text: All three GDL stages forbid hand-held and hands-free phones and every other electronic device.

memory_support.text: Late night off, phone down always.

prompt.text: Eli left his letterhead certification in his locker. Can he drive home during the prohibited hours?

answer.text: No. He must carry the signed certification while driving during those hours.

rationale.text: The work exemption applies only while the driver carries the signed letterhead certification.

narration.text: Getting a permit or a probationary license is only half the story. While you hold one, New Jersey attaches rules to how you drive. This lesson covers when you may not be on the road at all, the narrow exemption for work and religious reasons, the ban on phones and other electronic devices, who may sit beside a permit holder as the supervising driver, who is responsible when a student commits an offense, and what can happen to a driver who ignores the restrictions. These rules apply across the GDL stages, so they show up again and again on practice questions.

lines.text: No driving eleven oh one pm to five am.
Covers examination permit and probationary holders.

narration.text: The first restriction is about the clock. Special learner permit holders, examination permit holders and probationary license holders may not drive between eleven oh one at night and five in the morning. Notice that all three stages are named. It is not only the youngest permit holders, and it does not end the day the probationary license arrives. The ban lasts through the probationary stage too. A useful way to picture it: a little after eleven at night, GDL drivers should already be parked, and they stay off the road until five in the morning. Questions often test whether probationary drivers are included. They are.

There is one exemption to the late-night ban, and it is narrower than people think. A permit or probationary driver under twenty-one may drive during the prohibited hours for work or religious reasons, but only while carrying a signed certification on the employer's or religious institution's official letterhead. The exemption covers only those prohibited hours. It is not a general pass from the other GDL rules. And the certification has to be in the car while the driver is driving during those hours. A letter left on the kitchen table does not count, and a spoken promise from a boss is not a signed certification.

The next rule is one of the simplest and one of the most tested. All three GDL stages forbid hand-held cell phones, hands-free cell phones and every other electronic device while driving. Many adult drivers are used to hands-free calling and assume it is fine for everyone. For GDL drivers, it is not. The ban covers the special learner permit, the examination permit and the probationary license alike. So a new driver may not take a hands-free call, may not use a device mounted on the dashboard, and may not reach for any other electronic gadget while driving. The rule has no exceptions in this section.

lines.text: Supervisor at least twenty-one, front seat.
Valid New Jersey license, three years' experience.

narration.text: A permit holder never drives alone. The supervising driver must sit in the front seat, be at least twenty-one, hold a valid New Jersey license and have at least three years of driving experience. All four conditions matter, so an older sibling with a fresh license or an adult who holds only an out-of-state license does not qualify. Responsibility is shared, too. If a student driver commits a traffic offense, both the student and the instructor or adult supervising driver are held responsible. And for anyone who ignores GDL restrictions, the consequence can be a one hundred dollar fine or a suspension of driving privileges.

lines.text: What must be in the car?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Eli is under twenty-one, holds a probationary license, and has a job that ends at midnight. He wants to drive himself home after his shift. He has a signed certification on his employer's official letterhead, but he usually leaves it in his locker. Can he drive home legally on a night when it stays in the locker? Work it out before reading on. No. The work exemption lets him drive during the prohibited hours only while carrying the signed letterhead certification. The exemption covers just those hours, and the certification has to be with him while he is driving then.

lines.text: Off the road late at night.
No phones or devices at all.

narration.text: Let us pull this lesson together. Special learner permit, examination permit and probationary license holders may not drive between eleven oh one pm and five am. A driver under twenty-one may drive in those hours for work or religion only while carrying a signed certification on official letterhead, and the exemption covers only those hours. All three stages ban hand-held and hands-free phones and every other electronic device. A supervising driver sits in front, is at least twenty-one, holds a valid New Jersey license and has three years of experience. Student and supervisor share responsibility, and ignoring GDL restrictions can mean a one hundred dollar fine or a suspension.

why_how.text: Passenger rules depend on which permit you hold, so name the permit before counting riders.
The age twenty-one footnote is a short, exact list, which is why phones and belts stay outside it.

scenario.text: Theo, with a probationary license and no dependents, wants to drive two friends with no parent along.

reasoning.text: His license allows dependents plus one other person unless a parent or guardian rides along.

result.text: He may take one friend; the second must find another ride.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking everything lifts at twenty-one, including the phone ban.

correction.text: Only the hour, passenger and decal restrictions lift; the footnote does not mention the phone ban or the seat belt rule.

prompt.text: Theo has a probationary license, no dependents and no parent along. How many friends may ride with him?

rationale.text: Probationary holders may carry dependents plus one other person unless a parent or guardian rides along.

lines.text: Belts, decals, and the age twenty-one change.

narration.text: This lesson is about who and what goes in and on a GDL driver's car. First, passengers: the special learner permit and the examination permit have different passenger limits, and that difference is one of the most common sources of mistakes. Then seat belts, which every person in the car must wear. Then the red reflective decals: where they go, how many there are and what extra pairs cost. Finally, the change that comes at age twenty-one for examination permit and probationary license holders, including the rules that the age twenty-one footnote does not mention. Pay close attention to the exact wording of each passenger rule.

Start with the special learner permit, the one used on the early bird road. A special learner permit holder may carry any parent, any guardian or any dependent, plus one additional passenger. So a permit holder practicing with a parent could also carry another parent, a dependent and one friend besides. The family members, meaning parents, guardians and dependents, form the allowed group, and the extra spot is for one person beyond them. Notice the word any. Every parent, guardian or dependent is welcome. That broad family allowance is what sets this permit apart from the examination permit we look at next.

lines.text: Limit lifts when a parent or guardian rides.

narration.text: Now the examination permit and the probationary license. Holders of these may carry their dependents plus one other person. That is narrower than the special learner rule, because it names only dependents, not every parent or guardian, as the family allowance. There is an exception that opens things up: the limit does not apply when a parent or guardian is riding along. So a probationary driver out with friends and no parent can carry only one of them, plus any dependents. With a parent or guardian in the car, that passenger limit no longer applies. The presence of a parent or guardian is the switch.

lines.text: Special learner: any parent, guardian or dependent, plus one.
Examination: dependents plus one, unless a parent rides.

narration.text: Here is where the passenger rules get swapped. A special learner permit allows any parent, guardian or dependent, plus one more passenger. An examination permit allows dependents plus one more, unless a parent or guardian rides along. Read those side by side and notice two differences. The special learner rule lists parents and guardians as part of the allowed group. The examination permit rule does not; instead, a riding parent or guardian lifts the limit. When a question describes a permit driver with passengers, first identify which permit it is. Then apply that permit's wording, not the other one.

lines.text: Driver and every passenger buckle up.
Red decal top left, rear plate.
Red decal top left, front plate.

narration.text: Two more rules apply to every GDL car. First, seat belts: the GDL driver and every passenger must wear one, front seat and back. Second, decals: they must be displayed on the license plates. GDL drivers under twenty-one put one red reflective decal on the top left corner of the rear license plate and one on the top left corner of the front plate. Two removable decals come with the permit for a four dollar fee, and if you need more, extra pairs cost four dollars at any MVC Licensing Center. So picture two small red markers, one high on the left of each plate.

When an examination permit or probationary license holder is twenty-one or older, three restrictions no longer apply: the hour restriction, the passenger restriction and the decal restriction. That is the whole list. The footnote that grants this lifts only those three. It does not mention the ban on phones and electronic devices, and it does not mention the seat belt rule. So an older driver on the adult road can drive late, carry more passengers and skip the decals, but the footnote gives no permission to use a phone or ride unbuckled. If a question offers phones or belts as something that lifts at twenty-one, that is the trap.

Here is a quick check: Theo is eighteen and holds a probationary license. He wants to drive two friends to the movies, and no parent or guardian is coming along. He has no dependents. How many of his friends may ride with him? Work it out before reading on. Only one. Probationary license holders, like examination permit holders, may carry their dependents plus one other person unless a parent or guardian rides along. With no parent or guardian in the car and no dependents, Theo's limit is one friend. The broader family rule he may remember belongs to the special learner permit, not to his license.

lines.text: Examination and probationary: dependents plus one.
At twenty-one: hours, passengers, decals lift.

narration.text: Let us pull this lesson together. A special learner permit holder may carry any parent, guardian or dependent plus one more passenger. Examination permit and probationary license holders may carry dependents plus one other person, unless a parent or guardian rides along. The GDL driver and every passenger wear seat belts, and the red reflective decals sit on the top left corner of both plates, two for a four dollar fee with extra pairs at four dollars. At twenty-one, examination permit and probationary holders lose the hour, passenger and decal restrictions, but the footnote does not mention phones or seat belts. Next, we turn to drivers arriving from elsewhere.

why_how.text: An existing license speeds things up, but newcomers still need a New Jersey examination permit on a deadline.
An International Driving Permit only adds identification and translation, so it must ride along with a valid license.

scenario.text: Omar becomes a permanent resident with an out-of-state license valid for two more years.

reasoning.text: The rule gives him sixty days after residency, or the expiration date if that comes first.

result.text: Sixty days comes first, so he buys his examination permit within sixty days and passes the vision screening.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing an International Driving Permit can replace a driver license.

correction.text: An IDP adds identification and translation, but a valid driver license must still be carried.

memory_support.text: Sixty days or expiry, whichever first.

prompt.text: Omar's old license is valid for two more years. Can he wait until it expires to buy his New Jersey examination permit?

answer.text: No. He must buy it within sixty days after becoming a permanent resident.

rationale.text: The deadline is sixty days or the old license's expiration, whichever happens first.

narration.text: Not every New Jersey driver starts from scratch. Some arrive with a license from another state, and some visit from another country with a foreign license. This lesson covers both groups. For people moving in from another state, we look at the examination permit they still need, the deadline for getting it, what happens to newcomers under eighteen and which tests they can skip. For visitors from abroad, we look at the International Driving Permit, where to get it and what it can and cannot do. The key idea throughout is that an existing license helps, but it does not let anyone skip every step.

lines.text: Examination permit needed even with a license.
Buy it within sixty days of residency.
Sooner if the old license expires first.

narration.text: A driver who moves to New Jersey with a valid license from another state still needs a driver examination permit. Holding a good license elsewhere does not remove that step. There is also a deadline. Drivers arriving from another state must purchase a New Jersey examination permit within sixty days after becoming permanent residents. If the old license expires before those sixty days run out, the deadline moves up to the expiration date, because the rule says whichever happens first. So the sixty days is a ceiling, not a guarantee. An old license that expires in a few weeks shortens the window.

lines.text: Under eighteen joins the GDL Program.
Knowledge and road tests can be waived.

narration.text: Age matters for newcomers too. Out-of-state drivers under eighteen who move to New Jersey fall under the GDL Program, so the graduated rules you have learned apply to them. For testing, every out-of-state applicant must pass a vision screening. The knowledge and road tests, though, are waived when the applicant has a valid non-probationary license or a certified driver abstract from any state, the District of Columbia or a US territory. Notice the word non-probationary. The waiver is tied to a non-probationary license or a certified driver abstract, so read the license type in any question carefully.

title.text: A permit is not a license

lines.text: Carry an IDP or English translation.
Get the IDP in your own country.
The IDP never replaces a license.

narration.text: Visitors from other countries face a different rule, and a common misunderstanding. Visitors with a foreign license should carry an International Driving Permit, often called an IDP, or an acceptable English translation. Non-citizens must get the IDP in their own country before traveling, not after they arrive. Here is the trap. An IDP is an official document, but it can never replace a driver license. It only adds identification and helps across language barriers. That means a visitor must still carry a valid driver license alongside the IDP. The IDP travels with the license; it never travels instead of it.

Here is a quick check: Omar moves from another state and becomes a permanent New Jersey resident this month. His old license is valid for two more years. He plans to wait until it expires before dealing with the MVC. Is that a good plan? Work it out before reading on. No. Drivers arriving from another state must buy a New Jersey examination permit within sixty days after becoming permanent residents, or when the old license expires if that comes first. For Omar, the sixty days arrive long before his expiration date, so sixty days is his deadline. And he needs that permit even though his old license is valid.

lines.text: Permit within sixty days, or at expiry.
Vision test; others waived with a license.
IDP adds to a license, never replaces.

narration.text: Let us pull this lesson together. A driver moving in with a valid out-of-state license still needs a New Jersey examination permit, bought within sixty days after becoming a permanent resident, or when the old license expires if that comes first. Newcomers under eighteen fall under the GDL Program. Every out-of-state applicant passes a vision screening, and the knowledge and road tests are waived with a valid non-probationary license or certified driver abstract. Visitors with a foreign license carry an International Driving Permit, obtained in their own country, or an English translation, and the IDP never replaces a driver license. Next, we look at ID cards and registries.

why_how.text: Several MVC services begin at fourteen, so the age alone does not tell you which service a question means.
Each registry has a narrow purpose, like Next-of-Kin contacts used only by police after a crash.

scenario.text: Ava, sixteen, holds only an MVC boat license and wants emergency contacts on file.

reasoning.text: The Next-of-Kin Registry accepts any MVC-issued license, permit or non-driver ID, including a boat license.

result.text: She registers her contacts online, and only police may use them after a crash.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a hearing-impaired license is marked with words, like organ donor.

correction.text: Organ donation adds the words organ donor, but a hearing-impaired license carries a numerical code verified by a physician or audiologist.

prompt.text: Ava holds only a New Jersey boat license. Can she register emergency contacts under Sara's Law?

answer.text: Yes. Any MVC-issued license, permit or non-driver ID qualifies, including a boat license.

rationale.text: The Next-of-Kin Registry is open to every MVC credential holder, and contacts can be registered online or by mail.

narration.text: Licensing offices do more than issue driver licenses. This lesson covers the other services that ride along with a visit to the MVC. We start with the non-driver ID card for people who do not drive. Then we look at three registries: organ and tissue donation, the Next-of-Kin Registry created under Sara's Law, and voter registration offered under federal law. Finally, we cover how a license is marked for a driver with hearing loss. Several of these start at the same age, fourteen, so watch for questions that swap who qualifies, what each registry stores and who is allowed to use that information.

lines.text: Given up when a license arrives.

narration.text: Anyone aged fourteen or older who does not have a valid driver license may apply for a non-driver ID card. It gives people who do not drive a way to carry identification issued by the MVC. There is a catch when life moves on. The non-driver ID card must be given up when the person receives a New Jersey driver license. A person does not keep both. So picture a fourteen-year-old who gets a non-driver ID, then years later earns a New Jersey license. At that moment, the ID card is surrendered, and the new license is the card that person carries from then on.

lines.text: Say yes; license shows organ donor.
Asked at fourteen and again at eighteen.

narration.text: Organ donation is a simple yes at the counter. Answering yes to organ donation at an MVC Licensing Center puts the words organ donor on your license. The question is asked more than once. At age fourteen, a non-driver ID applicant is asked about the Donate Life Registry, and the question comes again at eighteen when applying for an unrestricted license or renewing. Anyone fourteen or older can register as an organ and tissue donor. The family pays nothing, funeral arrangements are not affected, and organs are shared through a national list. Those three points answer the most common worries people have.

lines.text: Store emergency contacts with the MVC.
Used only by police after a crash.
Any MVC license, permit or ID, even boats.

narration.text: The Next-of-Kin Registry, known as Sara's Law, lets people aged fourteen or older store emergency contacts with the MVC. Those contacts have one purpose. They are used only by police, to reach the people you listed after a crash leaves you unable to communicate. The registry is open to holders of any MVC-issued license, permit or non-driver ID, and that even includes a boat license. You do not have to visit an office to sign up. Contacts can be registered online or by a mailed form. So the registry is broad in who can join, and narrow in who can use the information.

lines.text: Organ donor: words on the license.
Hearing loss verified by physician or audiologist.

narration.text: Two different license markings get mixed up. When you say yes to organ donation, the license carries the words organ donor. A hearing-impaired driver license works differently. It is for a hearing loss of forty-one decibels or more, and it is marked with a numerical code, not with words. It also needs verification by a physician or an audiologist. So if a question asks how a hearing-impaired license is identified, the answer is a numerical code, and the proof comes from a physician or audiologist. If it asks what organ donation adds to the license, the answer is the words organ donor.

lines.text: Required by the National Voter Registration Act.

narration.text: One more service comes from federal law. Under the National Voter Registration Act, motor vehicle offices must offer voter registration. The offer goes to anyone applying for a license or ID, anyone renewing a license or ID, and anyone changing an address. That is a wide net. A first-time license applicant, someone renewing after years of driving and someone who just moved across town all hear the same offer. The rule is about the office making the offer. It applies whether the person came in for a driver license or a non-driver ID, and whether the visit is new, a renewal or an address update.

Here is a quick check: Ava is sixteen. She does not drive a car, but she holds a New Jersey boat license issued by the MVC. Her parents want her emergency contacts on file in case of a crash. Can Ava use the Next-of-Kin Registry, and does she have to go to an office? Work it out before reading on. Yes, she can join. The registry is open to holders of any MVC-issued license, permit or non-driver ID, including a boat license, and she is over fourteen. She does not need an office visit, because contacts can be registered online or by a mailed form. Only police will use them.

Let us pull this lesson together. Anyone fourteen or older without a valid driver license may get a non-driver ID card, which is given up once a New Jersey license arrives. Saying yes to organ donation puts the words organ donor on the license; the question comes at fourteen and again at eighteen, and the family pays nothing. The Next-of-Kin Registry under Sara's Law stores emergency contacts for police use only and is open to any MVC license, permit or ID holder. Motor vehicle offices must offer voter registration, and a hearing-impaired license carries a verified numerical code. Next, we finish with commercial licenses.

why_how.text: Every commercial class sits on top of a basic license, so Class D or an out-of-state CDL comes first.
The towed weight separates Class A from Class B, and passenger counts help define Classes B and C.

scenario.text: Dee holds a basic Class D license and wants to drive a school bus.

reasoning.text: Her Class D lets her apply for a commercial class, and a school bus driver needs both S and P.

result.text: She seeks the P endorsement, with its road test, age and experience rules, along with S.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating restriction L as an endorsement that adds a privilege.

correction.text: Restriction L takes a privilege away: the driver may not operate a vehicle equipped with air brakes.

memory_support.text: D first, then A, B, C.

prompt.text: Dee wants to drive a school bus. Is the passenger endorsement P enough?

answer.text: No. A school bus driver needs both the S and the P endorsements.

rationale.text: The school bus rule calls for S together with P.

narration.text: The last part of this section looks past the everyday car license to commercial driving. New Jersey has three commercial license classes, and each one is defined by vehicle weight, what is being towed or how many passengers ride. On top of the classes come endorsements, which add specific privileges, and restrictions, which take one away. You do not need to master commercial driving for a basic license, but it helps to know how the classes relate to the basic Class D license and what the most common letters mean. All commercial testing comes from a separate manual, so here we stay with the overview.

lines.text: Need a basic Class D first.

narration.text: There are three commercial license classes: A, B and C. None of them can be applied for without a valid basic Class D New Jersey license or a valid out-of-state CDL. So the commercial classes sit on top of a basic license; they do not replace it. Class A is the broadest. It also covers Classes B, C and D, as long as the driver has the proper endorsements. That means a Class A holder with the right endorsements can drive vehicles from the lower classes too. When a question asks what someone needs before applying for any commercial class, the answer is a valid basic Class D license or an out-of-state CDL.

lines.text: Class A: heavy combination, towed over ten thousand.
Class B: heavy vehicle, trailer ten thousand or less.
Class C: lighter hazmat, buses, eight to fifteen for hire.

narration.text: The weight lines between the classes are where most mix-ups happen. A Class A license is needed for a tractor trailer or other combination rated at twenty-six thousand one pounds or more when the towed vehicle is rated above ten thousand pounds. A Class B license covers any vehicle rated at twenty-six thousand one pounds or more, including one towing a trailer rated at ten thousand pounds or less, and buses that size built for sixteen or more passengers counting the driver. Class C covers lighter vehicles placarded for hazardous material, buses under that weight built for sixteen or more passengers, and vehicles carrying eight to fifteen passengers for hire.

lines.text: Farmers within one hundred fifty miles; personal RVs.

narration.text: Not every large or special vehicle calls for a commercial license. Several groups of drivers do not need a CDL. Taxi drivers are on the list, and so are drivers in a funeral procession. Operators of rescue and firefighting apparatus do not need one either. Farmers hauling within one hundred fifty miles of their farms are exempt, and so are people driving a recreational vehicle for personal use. Notice the conditions built into two of these. The farmer exemption depends on staying within one hundred fifty miles of the farm, and the RV exemption depends on the vehicle being for personal use. Read those conditions carefully in any question.

lines.text: P needs road test, twenty-one, three years.
School bus: both S and P.
H needs knowledge test, twenty-one, retests every two years.

narration.text: Endorsements add privileges to a commercial license. The passenger endorsement, P, requires a road test, an age of twenty-one and three years of driving experience. A school bus driver needs both the S and the P endorsements, not just one. The hazardous materials endorsement, H, requires a knowledge test, an age of twenty-one, and training with retesting every two years. The tanker endorsement, N, requires a knowledge test. A restriction works the other way. Restriction L means the driver may not operate a vehicle equipped with air brakes. All CDL tests come from the separate Commercial Driver Manual, not from this one.

Here is a quick check: Dee holds a basic Class D New Jersey license and wants to drive a school bus. She has learned that the passenger endorsement P requires a road test, an age of twenty-one and three years of driving experience. Is the P endorsement all she needs on her commercial license for the school bus? Work it out before reading on. No. A school bus driver needs both the S and the P endorsements. Her basic Class D license is what lets her apply for a commercial class at all, but the school bus calls for S together with P, not P alone.

lines.text: Class D or out-of-state CDL first.
A, B and C by weight and passengers.
P, S, H, N endorsements; L restriction.

narration.text: Let us pull this lesson together. There are three commercial license classes, A, B and C, and each requires a valid basic Class D New Jersey license or a valid out-of-state CDL first. Class A covers heavy combinations whose towed vehicle is rated above ten thousand pounds, and it also covers B, C and D with endorsements. Class B covers heavy vehicles and large buses, and Class C covers lighter hazmat vehicles, smaller buses and vehicles carrying eight to fifteen for hire. Taxi, funeral, rescue, nearby farm and personal RV drivers need no CDL. P and S cover school buses, H needs retesting, and L bars air brakes.
